## Important caveats before the numbers

**1. This is not a true unit-cost comparison.** The standard airline cost-efficiency metric is CASM (operating cost per available seat mile), but the source excerpts contain no capacity/ASM data — a search for available seat miles returned no matching passages. What follows is therefore a **cost-to-revenue** comparison, which blends cost discipline with pricing power (a premium-heavy network can look "efficient" on this basis while having high absolute unit costs). On a true CASM basis, Southwest — the worst performer below — has historically been among the *lowest* unit-cost carriers of this group because of its short-haul, single-fleet model.

**2. Alaska's FY2024 is not comparable to its own prior periods or cleanly to the others.** Alaska closed the Hawaiian acquisition on September 18, 2024, and "the results of Hawaiian are included in the consolidated financial statements beginning September 18, 2024... revenue and net loss from Hawaiian recognized in the Company's consolidated results of operations was $869 million and $113 million" [alaska_10k_note_acquisition.txt]. So Alaska's figures are a stub-period blend of two carriers, including merger-related dis-synergies.

**3. Fiscal alignment is fine:** all five are calendar-year filers, "Jan 1 – Dec 31" [airlines_costs_fy2024.txt].

## The data (FY2024, $M)

| | Revenue | Op. income | Implied opex | Opex/Rev | Op. margin | Labor/Rev | Fuel/Rev |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Delta | 61,643 | 5,995 | 55,648 | **90.3%** | **9.7%** | **26.2%** | **17.1%** |
| United | 57,063 | 5,096 | 51,967 | 91.1% | 8.9% | 29.2% | 20.6% |
| American | 54,211 | 2,614 | 51,597 | 95.2% | 4.8% | 29.6% | 21.1% |
| Alaska | 11,735 | 570 | 11,165 | 95.1% | 4.9% | 30.6% | 21.4% |
| Southwest | 27,483 | 321 | 27,162 | 98.8% | 1.2% | 44.5% | 21.1% |

Sources: Delta rev $61,643M / fuel $10,566M / labor $16,161M / op. income $5,995M; United $57,063M / $11,756M / $16,678M / $5,096M; Southwest $27,483M / $5,812M / $12,240M / $321M [airlines_costs_fy2024.txt]; American $54,211M / $11,418M / $16,021M / $2,614M; Alaska $11,735M / $2,506M / $3,588M / $570M [airlines_costs_fy2024.txt].

## Interpretation

Delta converts the largest share of revenue into operating profit, spending only ~90.3 cents of opex per revenue dollar. Its edge is concentrated in the two largest cost lines: labor at 26.2% of revenue (lowest of the five) and fuel at 17.1% (lowest by ~3.5 points, reflecting the Trainer refinery offset and a longer-stage-length, wide-body-weighted network). Delta and United are clearly ahead of American and Alaska (~95%), while Southwest is the outlier at 98.8% opex/revenue, with labor alone consuming 44.5% of revenue and labor-plus-fuel equal to 66.5% of total operating costs versus 48.0% at Delta.

The honest reading: Delta wins on cost *leverage* and profitability, but part of that is revenue-side premium mix rather than lower unit costs. Southwest's poor showing here reflects a revenue/capacity problem (and Boeing delivery delays) layered on a cost base that is structurally low per seat-mile — not evidence that it is the highest-unit-cost carrier.

ANSWER: Delta Air Lines — on the only cost basis computable from these filings (operating expense as a share of revenue), Delta was most efficient at ~90.3% opex/revenue (9.7% operating margin), with the lowest labor (26.2%) and fuel (17.1%) intensity; United ~91.1%, Alaska ~95.1%, American ~95.2%, Southwest ~98.8%. Note this is a cost-to-revenue proxy, not CASM (no ASM data in the filings provided), and Alaska's FY2024 includes Hawaiian only from September 18, 2024.
